data: If consumers in developed markets had been consuming corn flakes with cold milk for decades, why should a brand like Kellog’s advertise that cornflakes should be taken with hot milk, almost two decades after its entry into India? Why should a brand like Surf (or for that matter most detergent brands) weave a “story” around its brand with a drama-like ad? Why should Indian brands spend so much on cricket or film celebrities”[1]. Consumer behaviour is a fascinating subject. The course is not meant for addressing the above illustrative questions but for making you learn concepts that can come of help in thinking about how to approach such questions. Aren’t we all consumers, whether we snack on a samosa or go to a gym? Consumer behaviour is “the study of consumer’s actions during searching for, purchasing, using, evaluating, and disposing of products and services that they expect will satisfy their needs”[2]. At the end of the course, you should know the consumer decision-making model, with its stages and their respective elements: input (e.g., marketing mix, sociocultural influences), process (e.g., need recognition, information search, evaluation), output (e.g., purchase, use, post-purchase evaluation). Mastery of the subject will give you an edge for pursuing dream jobs in brand management, advertising, and consumer research. Not only that, but you can also pursue higher studies and path-breaking research.
